strings.glossary_adhan_def: The call to prayer, given aloud when the time for each of the five daily prayers comes in. A second, shorter call — the iqama — is given just before the prayer begins. Both are sunna for the prescribed prayers, even for someone praying alone.
strings.glossary_awrah_def: The part of the body that must be kept covered. For a man it is at least the area from the navel to the knees; for a woman in prayer it is the whole body apart from the face and the hands. Keeping it covered is a condition for the prayer to be valid. The schools draw the exact limits differently — a woman’s feet especially — and this guide does not set every one of them out.
strings.glossary_awrah_src: Reliance of the Traveller, f5.1, f5.3
strings.glossary_dhikr_def: Remembrance of Allah: short set phrases said to keep Him in mind — “subhan Allah” (glory be to Allah), “al-hamdu lillah” (praise be to Allah), “Allahu akbar” (Allah is greatest), and the like. After each obligatory prayer it is recommended to say a set of these, commonly thirty-three times each.
strings.glossary_dua_def: A personal prayer in your own words — asking Allah for something, or thanking Him. Unlike the salah, whose wording and timing are fixed, a du’a may be made at any moment and in any language, though the supplications the Prophet ﷺ taught are the best to use. The qunut said while standing in the prayer is one example.
strings.glossary_editions: Where a term’s ruling differs by school, each position is cited to a manual of that school: Reliance of the Traveller for Shafi’i, Nur al-Idah for Hanafi, The Risala for Maliki, Umdat al-Fiqh for Hanbali. Plain meanings not disputed between the schools are cited to Reliance.
strings.glossary_fard_aka: fardh, farz, fard al-ayn, fard al-kifaya, obligatory
strings.glossary_fard_def: An act the Sacred Law strictly requires. Doing it earns reward; leaving it without excuse is a sin, and within an act of worship it normally makes the whole act invalid — a prayer missing its bowing or a prostration does not count. A duty on every individual (the five daily prayers) is fard al-‘ayn; one that is discharged once enough people do it (the funeral prayer) is fard al-kifaya.
strings.glossary_fard_n1: Two distinct ranks. Fard is fixed by proof that is certain — the Qur’an, or a hadith reported through many chains; wajib rests on proof open to interpretation, such as a single-chain hadith. On this reckoning reciting the Fatiha is wajib, not fard: leaving it out forgetfully is mended by the forgetfulness prostration rather than voiding the prayer, and denying it is sinful but not disbelief.
strings.glossary_fard_n1_src: Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — The Wajib Elements Of Prayer
strings.glossary_fard_n2: The same word, with one exception in the pilgrimage. Every condition and integral of an act of worship is simply “obligatory”, with no rank in between.
strings.glossary_fard_n3: Treated as the same in practice; Maliki works even write “obligatory sunna” for firmly settled acts. The ranks that carry weight are obligatory (fard), confirmed sunna, and merit (fadila).
strings.glossary_fard_n4: This manual keeps a middle rank: seven mandatory acts (wajibat) — among them the first tashahhud and the tasbih of bowing — sit between the twelve pillars and the merely preferable acts. It notes that most scholars outside the school count those seven as only preferable.
strings.glossary_fard_n4_src: Umdat al-Fiqh (Ibn Qudamah), Book 2 ch. 5: The Pillars of Prayer and Its Mandatory and Recommended Acts
strings.glossary_fard_src: Reliance of the Traveller, c2.1, c3.2
strings.glossary_fatiha_aka: al-fatiha, fatihah, al-fatihah, umm al-kitab, the opening
strings.glossary_fatiha_def: The opening chapter of the Qur’an — “The Opening”, seven short verses — recited standing in every raka’ah of every prayer. Whether it counts as a pillar of the prayer or as a strongly required act, and what to do if it is missed, differs by school; the Mistakes guide sets that out.
strings.glossary_fatiha_src: Reliance of the Traveller, f8.1, f9.14
strings.glossary_ghusl_def: The full-body ritual washing that restores purity after a state of major impurity — sexual discharge, and the end of menstruation or of postnatal bleeding. Until it is done the prayer may not be prayed. You wash away any filth, perform wudu, then pour water over the whole body so none of the skin or hair is left dry.
strings.glossary_imam_def: The person who leads a congregational prayer. Everyone behind follows his movements and does not run ahead of him, and if he makes a mistake his forgetfulness prostration is followed by the whole row. Any sane adult male Muslim who prays soundly may lead; the most learned present has the first claim to.
strings.glossary_imam_src: Reliance of the Traveller, f8.1; The Risala (Ibn Abi Zayd al-Qayrawani), 11.1a
strings.glossary_intro: Terms you will meet all through this app and in the mosque, in plain English. Where a word means different things to different schools of law, the entry says so rather than pick one. Tap a linked term to jump to it; use the search box to find a spelling you know.
strings.glossary_itidal_aka: itidaal, i’tidaal, qawma, standing after ruku
strings.glossary_itidal_def: The upright pause after rising from the bowing and before going down into prostration. While rising you say “sami‘a llahu li-man hamidah” (Allah hears whoever praises Him), and standing straight, “rabbana laka l-hamd”. In the Shafi‘i school straightening up, and coming to rest in it, are integrals of the prayer.
strings.glossary_itidal_src: Reliance of the Traveller, f8.31, f9.14
strings.glossary_jamaah_def: The congregation — praying together in a group behind an imam rather than alone. It carries far more reward than praying by yourself. The schools weigh how binding it is differently, from a strongly confirmed sunna to a duty on every individual man; this guide does not set out each position.
strings.glossary_madhab_aka: madhhab, mazhab, mathhab, school of law, school of thought
strings.glossary_madhab_def: A school of Islamic law: a worked-out body of rulings running back to one of the early master-jurists and the scholars who refined his method. Most Sunnis follow one of four — Hanafi, Shafi’i, Maliki, Hanbali. They agree on the essentials and differ over details; this app marks each school’s position wherever the four part ways, and the madhab setting in Settings selects yours.
strings.glossary_muwalat_def: Doing the parts of an act one straight after another, with no long gap. It matters most in wudu, where the schools disagree over whether an unbroken sequence is actually required — the Wudu guide lays that out. In the prayer, a long deliberate pause with no reason breaks the continuity the prayer needs.
strings.glossary_nafl_aka: nafila, nafilah, naafila, mustahabb, mandub, tatawwu’, voluntary
strings.glossary_nafl_def: A voluntary prayer or act — one that earns reward when done and is no sin to leave. It runs from the sunna prayers attached to the five daily prayers to any extra prayer you choose to offer. Also called nafila, and, when specially encouraged, mustahabb.
strings.glossary_nafl_src: Reliance of the Traveller, c2.2; Nur al-Idah — The Rulings Pertaining To Jurisprudence [Fiqh]
strings.glossary_niyyah_def: The intention, settled in the heart, to perform a particular act of worship for Allah. For the prayer it must be there as you say the opening “Allahu akbar” — you fix in mind which prayer it is; saying it aloud is not required. For wudu the schools classify the intention differently, which the Wudu guide covers.
strings.glossary_niyyah_src: Reliance of the Traveller, f8.3, f9.14
strings.glossary_qada_def: A prayer offered after its appointed time has passed, to make it up — as against ada, a prayer done on time. A prayer missed through sleep or forgetfulness is made up when you realise; a new Muslim does not make up the prayers of the years before Islam. The Missed Prayers guide covers the rest — how soon, in what order, and where the schools differ.
strings.glossary_qibla_aka: qiblah, kiblah, kabah direction, direction of prayer
strings.glossary_qibla_def: The direction of prayer: towards the Kaaba in Mecca. Facing it is a condition for a valid obligatory prayer, set aside only in a few cases such as grave danger or a voluntary prayer offered while travelling. The app’s Qibla compass points the way.
strings.glossary_rakaah_aka: rak’ah, rakah, rakat, raka’at, rakaat, cycle
strings.glossary_rakaah_def: One full unit of the prayer: standing and reciting, then the bowing, the brief stand after it, and the two prostrations with a short sitting between them. Prayers are counted in raka’at — Fajr is two, Maghrib three, and Dhuhr, Asr and Isha four.
strings.glossary_ruku_def: The bowing: bending from the waist until the back is level and the hands rest on the knees, saying “subhana rabbiya l-‘azim” (glory to my Lord the Mighty), usually three times. Bowing is a pillar of the prayer in every school. How much the stillness within it is required — an integral, or a wajib — the Mistakes guide sets out.
strings.glossary_ruku_src: Reliance of the Traveller, f8.29, f9.14
strings.glossary_sahw_aka: sahu, sujood as-sahw, sujud as-sahw, forgetfulness prostration
strings.glossary_sahw_def: Forgetfulness or absent-mindedness in the prayer. Its remedy is sujood as-sahw — two extra prostrations that repair many, though not all, slips. The Mistakes guide covers when they are owed, how to perform them, and where the schools differ.
strings.glossary_salah_def: The formal Islamic prayer: a fixed sequence of standing, bowing, prostrating and sitting, with set recitation, performed five times a day at appointed times. It is the second pillar of Islam and the first thing a person is asked about on the Day of Judgement. Distinct from du’a, which is free supplication. This whole app teaches the salah.
strings.glossary_salah_src: Reliance of the Traveller, f1.1; The Risala (Ibn Abi Zayd al-Qayrawani), 40.03
strings.glossary_salam_def: The greeting of peace — “as-salamu ‘alaykum wa rahmatu llah” — turned to the right and then to the left, that ends the prayer. Saying it at least once, while seated, is what formally closes the prayer: the point after which ordinary speech and movement are allowed again. The schools rank exactly how obligatory it is a little differently.
strings.glossary_salam_src: Reliance of the Traveller, f8.47; The Risala (Ibn Abi Zayd al-Qayrawani), 40.03
strings.glossary_salawat_aka: salawaat, durood, darood, blessings on the Prophet, salat ala an-nabi
strings.glossary_salawat_def: Calling down Allah’s blessing on the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ — the “Allahumma salli ‘ala Muhammad…” said in the final sitting, after the tashahhud. Reliance counts it among the prayer’s six main sunnas: left out forgetfully, it calls for the forgetfulness prostration.
strings.glossary_salawat_src: Reliance of the Traveller, f8.45, f9.15
strings.glossary_src_reliance: Reliance of the Traveller (Umdat al-Salik), Ahmad ibn Naqib al-Misri, tr. Nuh Ha Mim Keller — Shafi’i, and the source for plain meanings the schools share.
strings.glossary_src_risala: The Risala, Ibn Abi Zayd al-Qayrawani, tr. Bello Mohammad Daura — Maliki.
strings.glossary_src_umdah: Umdat al-Fiqh, Ibn Qudamah al-Maqdisi, tr. and comm. Hatem al-Haj — Hanbali.
strings.glossary_sujood_def: The prostration: forehead and nose, both palms, both knees and the toes on the ground, saying “subhana rabbiya l-a‘la” (glory to my Lord the Most High). It is a pillar of the prayer in every school, done twice in each raka’ah with a sitting between. See also sahw, for the prostration of forgetfulness.
strings.glossary_sujood_src: Reliance of the Traveller, f8.33, f9.14
strings.glossary_summary: The words used in this app, defined
strings.glossary_sunnah_def: Two linked senses. First, the way of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ — what he said, did and approved — which together with the Qur’an is the foundation of the Law. Second, a ruling grade: an act the Law encourages without strictly demanding, so doing it earns reward and leaving it is no sin (though dropping a stressed sunna is blameworthy). The schools grade the recommended acts a little differently — see Fard.
strings.glossary_sunnah_src: Reliance of the Traveller, c2.2; Nur al-Idah — The Rulings Pertaining To Jurisprudence [Fiqh]
strings.glossary_surah_def: A chapter of the Qur’an; there are 114, ranging from three verses to nearly three hundred. In the first two raka’at of a prayer a short surah, or a few verses, is recited after the Fatiha.
strings.glossary_taawwudh_aka: taawwudh, ta’awwudh, taawudh, isti’adha, istiadha, a’udhu billah
strings.glossary_taawwudh_def: Saying “a‘udhu billahi mina sh-shaytani r-rajim” — “I seek refuge with Allah from Satan the outcast” — quietly, after the opening supplication and before the Fatiha, in the first raka’ah. Also called the isti‘adha.
strings.glossary_tahajjud_aka: tahajud, qiyam al-layl, night prayer, night vigil
strings.glossary_tahajjud_def: Voluntary prayer offered at night, after sleeping — a confirmed sunna, and the most meritorious prayer after the obligatory ones. The last third of the night is its best time. It is often prayed together with witr.
strings.glossary_tahmid_aka: tahmeed, alhamdulillah, al-hamdu lillah, hamd, hamdala
strings.glossary_tahmid_def: Praising Allah with the words “al-hamdu lillah” (praise be to Allah). It is one of the phrases said thirty-three times after each obligatory prayer, paired with “subhan Allah” (tasbih) and “Allahu akbar” (takbir); it is also the answer given while rising from the bowing — “rabbana laka l-hamd”.
strings.glossary_takbir_aka: takbeer, takbiratul ihram, takbiratul-ihram, allahu akbar
strings.glossary_takbir_def: Saying “Allahu akbar” — “Allah is greater”. The opening takbir (takbiratu l-ihram), said with the hands raised, is the integral that begins the prayer; a further takbir marks each move down into and up out of the bowing, the prostrations and the sittings.
strings.glossary_takbir_src: Reliance of the Traveller, f8.1, f9.14
strings.glossary_tartib_def: Keeping the parts of an act in their set order. In the prayer the integrals must follow their fixed sequence. In wudu — face, then arms, then head, then feet — the schools disagree over whether that order is itself required; the Wudu guide sets that out.
strings.glossary_tasbih_aka: tasbeeh, subhanallah, subhan allah, tasbihat, misbaha
strings.glossary_tasbih_def: Glorifying Allah with the words “subhan Allah” (glory be to Allah). It is the phrase said in the bowing and in the prostration, and one of the set said thirty-three times after each obligatory prayer, paired there with “al-hamdu lillah” (tahmid) and “Allahu akbar” (takbir). A string of beads for counting it is also called a tasbih.
strings.glossary_tashahhud_def: The sitting near the end of the prayer where you recite the testimony — “greetings to Allah… I bear witness that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad ﷺ is His Messenger” — lifting the index finger at the witness. A four-raka’ah prayer has a first, brief tashahhud after the second raka’ah and a final one at the end. Sitting for the final tashahhud is required in every school; how obligatory reciting the words is varies.
strings.glossary_tashahhud_src: Reliance of the Traveller, f8.45, f9.14; The Risala (Ibn Abi Zayd al-Qayrawani), 40.03
strings.glossary_tayammum_def: Dry purification: when water cannot be found, or cannot safely be used, you may wipe clean earth or dust over the face and the hands in place of wudu or ghusl, and pray. It lifts the barrier to prayer without removing the impurity itself, and lapses as soon as water is available.
strings.glossary_unreviewed: No qualified scholar has checked this glossary. Each definition that makes a legal point was checked against a manual and names where — but that verifies the wording, not the fiqh. Treat it as a draft and ask someone qualified before you rely on it.
strings.glossary_wajib_def: Literally “required”. For three of the four schools it is just another word for fard. The Hanafi school makes it a rank of its own: binding, but resting on evidence short of absolutely conclusive — so denying it is not disbelief, and leaving it forgetfully is repaired by the forgetfulness prostration rather than voiding the prayer. Witr and reciting the Fatiha are Hanafi examples. See Fard.
strings.glossary_wajib_src: Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — The Wajib Elements Of Prayer; Reliance of the Traveller, c2.1
strings.glossary_witr_def: An odd-numbered prayer — one, three or more raka’at, always ending on an odd count — offered after the Isha prayer and before dawn. It is the last prayer of the night. Its smallest form is a single raka’ah.
strings.glossary_witr_n1: Wajib — necessary, in Abu Hanifa’s ruling; not to be left. Three raka’at joined under a single closing salam, with the Fatiha and a surah in each.
strings.glossary_witr_n1_src: Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — The Chapter Of Witr
strings.glossary_witr_n2: A stressed voluntary (sunna) prayer, not an obligation. Its shortest valid form is one raka’ah; three or more are better, finishing with salams after each pair.
strings.glossary_witr_n3: A strongly confirmed sunna — the Risala’s summary calls it an “obligatory sunna” — of one raka’ah, preceded by an even-numbered voluntary prayer (the shaf‘).
strings.glossary_witr_n4: A strongly emphasised voluntary prayer, the most stressed of the night prayers; the least is one raka’ah and the fullest is eleven, with qunut after the bowing.
strings.glossary_witr_n4_src: Umdat al-Fiqh (Ibn Qudamah), Book 2 ch. 7: Supererogatory Prayers
strings.glossary_wudu_def: The ablution done before prayer: washing the face, then the arms to the elbows, wiping the head, and washing the feet to the ankles. It is required for a valid prayer and is broken by, among other things, using the toilet, breaking wind and deep sleep. The Wudu guide covers it in full, including the points where the schools differ.
